notes.h: Types of leisure facility in the community (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Leisure facilities in a community come from three kinds of provider: public bodies, commercial businesses and voluntary groups. Each is paid for and run differently, and that shapes the cost, range and condition a user can expect.
points: Public facilities are often provided or part-funded by local authorities (councils). They include swimming pools, leisure centres, libraries, parks, playgrounds, sports pitches, walking and cycling trails, community halls and arts centres.
Commercial facilities are private businesses run for profit, such as gyms and private health clubs, cinemas, bowling alleys, golf clubs, cafés and entertainment venues.
Commercial facilities depend on fees from users for their income, so the fee charged must cover running costs and make a profit.

Voluntary and community facilities are run by non-profit groups and volunteers. They include GAA clubs, soccer and tennis clubs, youth clubs, active retirement groups, drama and musical societies, and community centres.
Voluntary facilities are funded by membership fees, fundraising and grants, so they are not free: clubs usually charge a membership fee.
Voluntary facilities depend on volunteers and member subscriptions, so their range and condition vary from club to club.

Some facilities suit particular groups. Retired people, for example, often use golf, bingo, gym or leisure centre classes, library and book clubs, the swimming pool, the cinema, a choir or musical society, a drama group and card games.
notes.tip: Name the type of provider when you name a facility, and remember that a voluntary club still charges fees. Exams ask you to name and evaluate facilities popular with a group such as retired people.

notes.h: Criteria for evaluating a leisure facility (Higher Level only)
notes.b: An evaluation judges a facility against fixed criteria, so that two facilities can be compared on the same basis. A list of features is not an evaluation: you must weigh strengths against weaknesses for a particular user.
points: Cost: the fees charged, judged against what the user can afford, including membership and joining fees, pay-as-you-go charges, class fees, equipment, clothing, travel and concessions.
Value for money: the benefit the user gains, judged against the cost. It depends on how often the facility is used and whether it suits the user.
Location and accessibility: the ease of reaching the facility and using it, including distance, transport, parking and access for people with disabilities.

Range and quality: the number and variety of activities, such as pools, classes, courts or equipment, and the condition of the equipment. Classes should suit different ages and abilities, and there should be family provision.
Convenience: whether the opening hours and booking arrangements suit the user's working and family pattern. Crowding, waiting time and childcare on site also matter.
Safety, hygiene and staffing: clean changing rooms and equipment, qualified instructors and lifeguards, supervision during sessions, first aid, security and emergency procedures.
Atmosphere and suitability: whether the facility suits the user's age, gender, interests and ability, and whether it suits individual or family use.
Benefits: social (the chance to meet people and join groups, classes or teams), physical (fitness), emotional (relaxation) and intellectual (skill).
notes.tip: If asked for three criteria for choosing a leisure facility, pick from cost, value, accessibility, range, convenience, safety and staffing, or benefits. Link benefits to the facility, not to leisure in general.

notes.b: A facility is only useful if the person can reach it and use it at a time that suits them. Accessibility is about getting there and getting in, and convenience is about fitting the facility into daily life.
points: Location: a facility close to home or work reduces travel time and cost, so it is more likely to be used regularly.
Transport: the availability of buses or trains and the provision of parking affect how easily a user can get there.
Access for people with disabilities: ramps, lifts, accessible changing rooms and pool hoists allow people with mobility difficulties to use the facility.
Opening hours: early, late and weekend hours suit people who work or attend school during the day.
Booking systems: online booking and advance booking of classes make it easier to plan use, while queues and walk-in only systems can discourage use.
Family access: facilities that allow children and adults to use the same area together make family leisure easier to organise.
On-site childcare, short waiting times and uncrowded sessions also make a facility more convenient to use.
notes.tip: If asked how a facility could improve access for older people or people with disabilities, give specific measures such as ramps, lifts, accessible changing rooms, hoists, extended hours or online booking.

notes.h: Cost of using a facility (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The price on the door is only part of what a facility costs. To judge it fairly you need to add up every kind of cost the user will meet over a period such as a year.
points: Membership fee: a regular fee, usually paid monthly or yearly, that gives unlimited or extended use of the facility.
Joining fee: a one-off payment made when a person first becomes a member of a facility.

Two types of charge a facility makes: fixed charges, such as a membership or joining fee, do not change with use, while variable charges, such as pay-as-you-go, class and equipment fees, rise with each visit.
Pay-as-you-go charge: a fee paid each time the facility is used, which suits people who visit only occasionally. Membership suits regular users.
Class and course fees: extra charges for instructor-led sessions, which are often separate from the basic entry or membership fee.
Concessions: reduced fees for students, children, older people, unemployed people and families, which lower the cost for these groups.
Hidden costs: travel, equipment, clothing, locker or towel hire, parking and refreshments add to the total cost of using a facility.
Total annual cost: the sum of membership or joining fees, pay-as-you-go charges, class fees, extras and travel for one year.
notes.tip: To explain the difference between membership and pay-as-you-go, say membership is a regular fee for ongoing use and pay-as-you-go is paid per visit, then say which suits regular and which suits occasional users.

notes.h: Value and value for money (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Cost is not the same as value. A low price does not make a facility good, because value compares what the user gains with what the user pays.
points: Value is the benefit a person gains from a facility, measured in fitness, enjoyment, social contact and skill.
Value for money is the benefit gained for each euro spent, so a cheap facility that is rarely used may offer poor value.
A facility offers more value when its range of activities matches the user's interests, and when the user actually uses those activities.
Cost per visit is found by dividing the total annual cost by the number of visits made in the year.
A low cost per visit shows that the facility is used often, which generally means better value for regular users.
Value depends on the user: a person who uses only the pool may find a high-fee gym poor value, even though it offers more activities.
A dearer facility used often may give better value than a cheap one used rarely, so value depends on use.
notes.tip: Never say a cheaper facility is automatically better value. Compare the benefit with the cost for the stated user, using cost per visit.

notes.h: Cost and value comparison of two facilities (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The syllabus asks for a cost and value comparison of two facilities. Follow the same steps each time so that the comparison is fair and ends in a justified conclusion for a named user or family.
points: Step 1: select two facilities that serve the same community and are used for the same purpose, such as fitness or swimming, for example a local authority leisure centre and a private gym, or a community club and a commercial club.
Step 2: find each facility's fees: membership, joining, pay-as-you-go and class fees. To investigate, list the facilities, visit them or check their websites, and collect the fees.
Step 3: calculate the total annual cost of each facility, including the travel cost of getting there.
Step 4: estimate the number of visits per year for the user, and divide the total annual cost by that number to find the cost per visit.

Step 5: list the benefits each facility gives the user, including fitness, social contact, relaxation and skill, and compare them with the cost. Also compare location, access, hours, range of activities, condition, safety, staffing and atmosphere.
Step 6: state which facility gives better value for the user, and say what would change the conclusion, such as a change in visits or income, or a different household member.
notes.tip: A good answer lists fees and extra costs, compares cost per visit, range, access and hours, and gives a justified conclusion. Any figures you use in a worked comparison are illustrative only (example only), for Facility A and Facility B.

notes.h: Evaluation judgement and improvements (Higher Level only)
notes.b: An evaluation ends in a judgement, not a list. You weigh each facility's strengths against its weaknesses for a particular user, then suggest how the facility could do better.
points: An evaluation weighs the strengths of each facility against its weaknesses, then reaches a judgement for a named type of user.
A facility with low fees but few activities may suit a student who wants cheap exercise, but not a family wanting varied activities.

When you name a facility, give two developed points, each a strength or a limit. For example, a swimming pool gives low-impact exercise and social contact for retired people, but may involve travel and set sessions.

Improvements a facility could make include extended opening hours, reduced fees or concessions for families and older people, better access for people with disabilities, and more classes for older people or families.
Improvements to booking and information, such as online booking and online timetables, make a facility easier to use and so raise its value.
notes.tip: When asked to evaluate a facility, name it and give a strength and a limit for each point, such as cost, access, social contact, health benefit and suitability for the user's age. Finish with a judgement and an improvement.

keyTerms.definition: A leisure facility provided and run by a local authority or other public body, such as a swimming pool or library.
A leisure facility run for profit, such as a private gym, cinema or golf club.
A leisure facility run by a non-profit group or club, such as a GAA club or community centre.
A regular payment that gives a person continued use of a leisure facility.
A system in which a user pays a fee each time they use a facility, rather than a membership fee.
A reduced fee offered to a group such as students, children, older people or unemployed people.
The ease with which a facility can be reached and used, including by people with disabilities.
The benefit gained from a facility in relation to the cost of using it.
The total annual cost of a facility divided by the number of visits made in the year.
A one-off payment made when a person first joins a leisure facility as a member.

factCards.term: Three types of leisure facility in a community
factCards.definition: 1. Public facilities, such as swimming pools, leisure centres and libraries. 2. Commercial facilities, such as gyms, cinemas and golf clubs. 3. Voluntary or community facilities, such as GAA clubs and community centres.

factCards.term: Four criteria for evaluating a leisure facility
factCards.definition: 1. Cost and value. 2. Accessibility. 3. Range of activities. 4. Safety, hygiene and staffing.

factCards.term: Two types of charge a leisure facility makes
factCards.definition: 1. Fixed charges, such as a membership fee or joining fee. 2. Variable charges, such as pay-as-you-go fees, class fees and equipment hire.

factCards.term: Three ways to improve the accessibility of a leisure facility
factCards.definition: 1. Extend opening hours to early mornings, evenings and weekends. 2. Offer concessions for families and older people. 3. Provide access for people with disabilities, such as ramps, lifts and accessible changing rooms.
The total annual cost of using the facility divided by the number of visits made in the year.

questions.prompt: Explain how to calculate the cost per visit of a leisure facility and state why this figure is useful when comparing two facilities.
questions.model: Calculation: add the membership or joining fees, pay-as-you-go charges, class fees and travel costs for one year to find the total annual cost, then divide that total by the number of visits made in the year. Usefulness: it allows two facilities with different fee structures to be compared on the same basis, and it shows whether a facility gives good value to a regular user. Both the method and the reason are needed for full marks.

questions.prompt: Evaluate two leisure facilities in your community, including a cost and value comparison. Refer to accessibility and the range of activities, and recommend which facility gives better value to a family of four.
questions.model: Two facilities identified, one public and one commercial or voluntary. Cost: fees for membership, joining, pay-as-you-go and classes, plus travel, totalled for one year and divided by the expected number of family visits to give cost per visit. Value: the benefits each facility gives, such as physical fitness, social contact and skill development for each family member, weighed against cost. Accessibility: location, transport, opening hours, booking arrangements and access for people with disabilities. Range of activities: whether the facility offers activities suited to all ages in the family, and whether they can be used together. Recommendation: the facility giving the lower cost per visit and the wider benefit for the family, with the reason stated and any improvements suggested, such as concessions for families or extended opening hours.
